summary: Round 1, test lane, on a decision-only commit (ADR-0036 plus backlog bookkeeping). No test to review, so I reviewed what the decision makes testable, and I verified by MEASUREMENT in my own tree rather than by reading. Answering the questions put to me. (1) DOES THE CHOSEN KEY ADMIT A DISCRIMINATING TEST? Partly, and it is vulnerable to the ADR's own rejection argument in a second form. The ADR rejects the lease-epoch alternative because it 'passes every test M4 can write' and breaks at M5. Its own mechanism -- one segment key per pod, 'the per-pod pointer' (l.68, l.83) -- has the same property, in both readings of the comparison it leaves unspecified: equality-only detection misses a replay of anything but a pod's most recent commit (double commit), and the order-based reading that is the natural successor to CheckpointWriter.java:129's Math::max suppresses a late-arriving but GENUINELY NEW key. Both are invisible at M4 because DefaultIngest.flushLocked (DefaultIngest.java:338-390) holds the lock and has exactly one commit outstanding per pod, and Sequencer's own contract already says a caller may not assume 'flushSeq values arrive in order'. F2. (2) CAN M4.10d WRITE A FAILING TEST FOR THIS DECISION TODAY, WITHOUT FIRST ADDING A RETRY PATH? YES -- at the Sequencer/LocalSequencer seam, not through DefaultIngest: commit(req) twice with the same CommitRequest, assert the second returns the ORIGINAL offsets and appends no second delta. That is red today (CommitLog.java:292-300's duplicate-key HashSet is per BATCH only, so a resubmission in a later window is accepted and assigned fresh offsets). The ADR's 'Nothing retries yet' paragraph (l.96-99) is honest and the second option it offers -- coverage stops at the sequencer seam -- is the one that works. F5 records the constraint it does not state: DefaultIngest's failure path discards `published`, so a producer-level retry mints a NEW key and the dedup never fires. (3) IS THE PRE-CHANGE-CHECKPOINT STATE REACHABLE, AND DOES A TEST FOR IT DISCRIMINATE? Reachable, and no -- a test asserting the replay is ACCEPTED is passed identically by a dedup that does nothing, and neither M4.10c's nor M4.10d's row requires it be paired with the post-upgrade REFUSAL on the same fixture. F4, minor: M4.10c's 'readers must accept BOTH versions' does constrain decode, which is the half that matters most. (4) DO THE M4.10 TRIPWIRES CHANGE? The doesNotContainKey one is already recorded as M4.10d's by round 10 of M4.10 and I am not re-raising it. But this ADR retires the OTHER one's subject -- aPodsFlushSeqNeverGoesBACKWARDSWhenAnOlderFlushArrivesLate exists solely to pin the Math::max fold on lastAppliedFlushSeq -- and no row says whether that field survives. F3. CLAIMS THAT CANNOT BE FALSIFIED BY A TEST, and whether that is acceptable here: 'the epoch stops discriminating when M5's forwarding lands' (l.24-27) is unfalsifiable today and ACCEPTABLE -- it is the ground for a rejection, not a property being relied on. 'No commit-path request scales with pods' (l.72) and 'Recovery reads no more than it does today' (l.59) are both falsifiable, the second one TODAY with CountingBinStore over ChainReplay.applyChain, and neither M4.10c's nor M4.10d's row asks for the request-count assertion -- worth one clause in whichever row lands the fold, not a finding here. The one claim that IS falsifiable and IS false is F1, and I measured it.

findings.title: MEASURED FALSE: a restarted pod does NOT reliably produce a different segment key, and under this repository's own ingest fixtures it produces a byte-identical one 87.5%-100% of the time -- so the decision's discriminating claim inverts into the harm the ADR exists to prevent
findings.failure_scenario: The ADR's whole discrimination rests on l.34-36: 'A restarted pod flushing new data produces a different key, because timestampMillis advances even though sequence restarts at 0.' I ran this in my review tree against the staged bytes. timestampMillis is Accumulator.firstAppendMillis (Accumulator.java:65, drain() at :126 passes it to writer.toByteArray), read back out of the segment at SegmentPublisher.java:110 and put into the key at :133; sequence is SegmentPublisher.java:53's instance AtomicLong, which restarts with the process. Two SegmentPublisher instances with the same podShortId and prefix, carrying DIFFERENT records, minted the identical key `bins/c/data/2023/11/14/22/0000001700000000000-pod7-0000000000000000-h49-A.bseg` -- 200/200 under a frozen clock, and 175/200 under Clock.systemUTC(), which is the clock IngestTestSupport.java:68 wires into every DefaultIngest fixture. So: the M4.10d test that asserts 'a restarted pod's first flush is ACCEPTED' cannot be written against the standard ingest fixture at all -- a CORRECT implementation of this ADR sees a byte-identical key and SUPPRESSES a real commit, which is the ADR's own stated primary harm ('worse than the duplication it exists to prevent', l.19-20). And a test that uses Clock.systemUTC() to dodge it is flaky at 87.5%. The ADR bounds segment-key collision to the out-of-protocol two-live-processes case in the ADR-0031 paragraph (l.88-94, 'timestamps colliding') and thereby asserts the IN-protocol restart is safe, without ever naming the precondition that makes it so: that firstAppendMillis never repeats across incarnations of one podShortId. That precondition is a wall-clock property, and testing.md rule 1 and non-negotiable 7 exist to keep exactly that class of assumption out of business logic. SegmentPublisher.java:135's 'put, not putIfAbsent -- the key is unique WITHOUT coordination' rests on the same assumption and today silently overwrites the segment OBJECT in that case; ADR-0036 promotes it from 'which object we overwrote' to 'which real commits we suppress'.
findings.suggestion: State the precondition on the decision itself: the key discriminates a restart only while the clock advances at least one millisecond between two incarnations' first appends, and say what M4.10c/d must do when it does not (refuse to dedup on a key whose timestamp is not strictly greater than the pod's recorded one, or fold the incarnation in somewhere that does not grow with history). Then say which clock M4.10d's restart fixture uses and why it must be stepped, so the next author does not reach for IngestTestSupport and conclude the decision is wrong.

findings.title: the window's DEPTH and its comparison are unspecified, and both readings are the exact 'passes every test M4 can write, breaks at M5' failure this ADR uses to reject the lease epoch
findings.failure_scenario: l.38-40 says the checkpoint carries 'per pod, enough to detect a replay'; l.62 says a leader harvests 'each pod's most recent segment key'; l.68 says 'One entry per pod, as today'; l.83 says 'the per-pod pointer'. That fixes the window at one key per pod but never says how an incoming key is compared to it, and the two available answers fail in opposite directions. (a) EQUALITY: only a replay of a pod's most RECENT commit is detected. A replay of anything older is accepted and committed twice -- the row's primary harm. Note the shape this drops: today's Map<String,Long> lastAppliedFlushSeq gives an UNBOUNDED-depth window from ONE number, because flushSeq is dense and monotone (M4.10a landed a whole task and CommitProtocolSimulationFlushSeqTest to guarantee 0..n-1 per pod), so `incoming <= stored` answers for every older commit at once. A single opaque key has no such property, and the ADR does not acknowledge losing it. (b) ORDER (the natural successor to CheckpointWriter.java:126-129's `pods.merge(podId, flushSeq, Math::max)`, whose own comment says 'a retried or late flush arrives with a [lower value]'): a late-arriving but genuinely NEW segment key from a live pod compares lower than the stored one and is suppressed -- again the primary harm. Sequencer.java's contract already says a caller may NOT assume 'flushSeq values arrive in order', and CheckpointWriterContentTest.aPodsFlushSeqNeverGoesBACKWARDSWhenAnOlderFlushArrivesLate (CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:116-129) exists precisely because 'a late or retried flush is exactly how that happens in production'. THE SURVIVING MUTATION: an M4.10c/d that stores one key per pod and detects by equality passes every test M4 can write, because DefaultIngest.flushLocked (DefaultIngest.java:338-390) holds the lock across publish-and-commit, so one pod never has two commits outstanding and never has an older un-replayed one. It is broken by the first M5 forwarding that pipelines two commits from one pod. That is verbatim the argument l.24-27 uses to reject qualifying the pair with the lease epoch. The discriminating test is writable TODAY at the sequencer seam and needs no M5: commitAll(List.of(podA/S1, podA/S2)) -- legal now, CommitLog.java:292-300 refuses only a shared segment KEY, not a shared podId -- then commit(podA/S1) again; a depth-one equality window accepts it, and CommitLog.java:329-334 appends a second delta assigning fresh offsets.
findings.suggestion: Say in the Decision section which of the two the dedup does, and state the precondition that makes it sufficient (e.g. 'at most one commit outstanding per pod, which M5's forwarding must preserve') -- or record that the per-pod entry carries the last N keys, which is still bounded by pods rather than history and satisfies ADR-0033 exactly as the pointer does. Then give M4.10d the two-deep fixture above as an acceptance criterion, so the depth is pinned by a test rather than by DefaultIngest happening to be serial.

findings.title: the ADR retires the subject of a landed tripwire without saying so, and neither the gate nor M4.10c's row would notice its deletion
findings.failure_scenario: l.53-56 describes `pods` as Map<String, Long> podId -> lastAppliedFlushSeq and says Checkpoint changes, but never says whether lastAppliedFlushSeq SURVIVES alongside the segment key or is replaced by it. CheckpointWriterContentTest.aPodsFlushSeqNeverGoesBACKWARDSWhenAnOlderFlushArrivesLate (CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:116-129) has exactly one subject: the Math::max fold at CheckpointWriter.java:129, killed by the `put` mutation its own comment names. If M4.10c replaces the value type, that test loses its subject and the cheapest resolution is deleting the whole method -- forbidden by non-negotiable 2 -- and check-test-integrity.sh cannot see it: a whole-method deletion leaves no weakened assertion to score, and M4.10c's new row (backlog.md) mentions neither the field nor the test. This is a DIFFERENT tripwire from the doesNotContainKey one that round 10 of M4.10 already assigned to M4.10d; this one is a new consequence of ADR-0036 and currently belongs to nobody. The successor property is cheap and well defined -- a segment key IS lexicographically chronological (SegmentKey.render zero-pads timestampMillis to 19 and derives the date path from the same value), so the max fold carries over intact -- which is why leaving it unstated costs more than saying it.
findings.suggestion: One clause in M4.10c's row: whether lastAppliedFlushSeq stays, and that aPodsFlushSeqNeverGoesBACKWARDSWhenAnOlderFlushArrivesLate is REWRITTEN against whatever replaces it, never deleted.

findings.title: the pre-change-checkpoint consequence is stated as ACCEPTED, and the only test of it is passed identically by a dedup that does nothing
findings.failure_scenario: l.80-87 accepts, rather than refuses, a replay against a window recovered from a v0 checkpoint. That state is reachable in a test (encode a v0 Checkpoint, seed it, take over, replay a commit) and the assertion would be 'the replay was accepted' -- which is satisfied by a correct implementation, by a dedup that is a no-op, and by one that never recovers the window at all. It discriminates only when the SAME fixture also runs the post-upgrade case and asserts the replay is REFUSED. M4.10c's new row carries only 'readers must accept BOTH versions (M3.0)', which is a decode assertion and does constrain something real; M4.10d's row carries the refusal but against a fresh checkpoint, not against the v0 pair. So the two halves exist in different rows and nothing requires them to share a fixture, which is the only arrangement in which either is worth having.
findings.suggestion: Add to M4.10c or M4.10d: the v0-recovered acceptance and the post-upgrade refusal are asserted in one test method against one fixture, differing only in which checkpoint was seeded.

findings.title: 'a retry resubmits the same published.key()' is true only of a retry placed inside flushLocked, and the ADR does not bound where the retry may live
findings.failure_scenario: DefaultIngest.flushLocked's catch (DefaultIngest.java:386-390) completes every waiter exceptionally and rethrows, so `published` -- the key and the bytes -- is discarded on an ambiguous commit failure. A producer that retries at the HTTP layer re-appends into a NEW Accumulator, which drains a NEW segment with a NEW createdAt and a NEW sequence, so the resubmitted key DIFFERS and the dedup never fires. The ADR's l.32-33 claim holds only for a retry placed INSIDE flushLocked, around sequencer.commit, holding the same `published`. l.96-99 correctly says nothing retries yet and hands M4.10d the choice, but not this constraint, so an M4.10d that adds the retry one layer up satisfies every word of the ADR and detects nothing. (It self-reveals as a double commit rather than as a false green, which is why this is minor rather than major.)
findings.suggestion: One sentence at l.99: if M4.10d adds the retry, it retries the SEQUENCER call holding the already-published segment, never the append.
